why_how.text: The brain cannot fully attend to two activities at once, so anything that takes your eyes, hands or mind from driving is a hazard.
Switching between tasks takes about a quarter second, and at sixty-five miles per hour that is twenty-four feet of travel.

scenario.text: Mia reaches to change the radio station while driving at sixty-five miles per hour on the expressway.

reasoning.text: Shifting attention takes about a quarter second, and in that time a car at sixty-five covers twenty-four feet.

result.text: Mia's car travels about twenty-four feet while her attention shifts, which is why even tuning a radio carries risk.

claim.text: Myth: a quick glance at the radio is harmless because it takes no time at all.

correction.text: The switch takes about a quarter second, and at sixty-five miles per hour the car covers twenty-four feet in that time.

prompt.text: Name the three things a distraction can pull away from driving.

answer.text: Your eyes from the road, your hands from the wheel, and your mind from driving.

rationale.text: Each one is a hazard because the brain cannot fully attend to two activities at once.

narration.text: This lesson explains why distracted driving is so dangerous, before we get to the rules that address it. Federal highway safety officials estimate at least three thousand four hundred deaths each year from crashes where a manual, visual or cognitive distraction pulled the driver's focus from controlling the vehicle. That number may even understate the problem, because it is hard to prove a distraction and its part in a crash. We will look at the three kinds of distraction, why the brain struggles with two tasks, and how far a car travels in a moment of switched attention.

Anything that pulls your eyes from the road, your hands from the wheel or your mind from driving is a hazard, because the brain cannot fully attend to two activities at once. That covers more than phones. Reaching for a drink, reading a sign about a sale, or replaying an argument in your head can all pull your focus. The three kinds often stack. Texting, for example, takes your eyes, your hands and your mind all at once. When you judge whether something is safe to do while driving, ask whether it takes any of those three away.

lines.text: Switching tasks takes about a quarter second.
At sixty-five, that is twenty-four feet.

narration.text: Your brain needs roughly a quarter second to switch between two tasks. In that time, a car going sixty-five miles per hour travels twenty-four feet. That is distance covered while your attention is not fully on the road. It may not sound like much, but it is more than the length of a car, and it happens every time you shift your focus back and forth. Repeated switches add up quickly. This is why the handbook treats even small tasks as risky at highway speed, and why planning ahead matters so much. Planning ahead is the best defense.

lines.text: Trap: a quick glance is harmless.
A quarter second covers twenty-four feet.

narration.text: Here is the trap. It is tempting to think a quick glance at the radio or a fast reach for a cup costs no time at all. It does. At sixty-five miles per hour a car covers twenty-four feet in the quarter second it takes to shift attention, so even tuning a radio carries risk. Another trap is the idea that only phones count as distraction. The handbook's rule is broader: anything that takes your eyes, hands or mind from driving is a hazard. Options that limit distraction to phones alone are missing the point. Read every option with that in mind.

Here is a quick check: name the three things a distraction can pull away from driving. Picture the driver's seat. The first is your eyes, pulled from the road. The second is your hands, pulled from the wheel. The third is your mind, pulled from the task of driving. Each one is a hazard on its own, because the brain cannot fully attend to two activities at once. If you named phones, that is an example rather than a category, and phones often take all three of these at the same time. Each one alone is enough to cause trouble.

lines.text: Twenty-four feet in a quarter second.

narration.text: To wrap up, distraction is any manual, visual or cognitive pull away from controlling the vehicle, and officials estimate at least three thousand four hundred deaths a year from it, a number that may be too low because distraction is hard to prove. The brain cannot fully attend to two tasks, and a quarter-second switch at sixty-five miles per hour covers twenty-four feet. A distracted driver who drives carelessly or negligently in a way likely to endanger people or property, or with willful or wanton disregard, can be prosecuted under Michigan law.

why_how.text: Most distractions can be handled before the trip, so setting things up first keeps your eyes, hands and mind on driving.
If you must make a call, parking safely first removes the distraction entirely.

scenario.text: Omar is driving alone to a new store and needs directions.

reasoning.text: The handbook says to plan your route in advance when driving alone, or have a front-seat passenger handle navigation.

result.text: Omar plans the route before he starts the car.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking it is fine to finish grooming at red lights.

correction.text: Grooming should be finished before starting out or after arriving, not while driving.

prompt.text: You are about to leave and your child is fussing in the back. When should you get them comfortable and buckled?

rationale.text: Tending to children while driving is a serious distraction, so settle them before you go.

narration.text: This lesson turns the danger of distraction into habits you can use every day. The handbook's advice falls into two groups. The first group is what to do before you start driving, so that fewer things compete for your attention later. The second group is what to avoid while the car is moving. Most of these habits are simple, but practice questions often test whether you know which tasks belong before the trip and which should never happen at all while driving. As we go, notice how many problems disappear with a little planning.

lines.text: Or plan the route in advance.

narration.text: Before driving, ask a front-seat passenger to handle maps or navigation, or plan your route in advance if you drive alone. Learn your vehicle's controls well enough to adjust temperature or radio settings without looking away from the road. Both habits take a visual task and remove it from the drive. Knowing where the controls are means your eyes can stay ahead of you even when you need to make a small change. And a route planned in advance means you are not searching for turns at the last moment while traffic moves around you.

lines.text: Groom before leaving or after arriving.

narration.text: Set radio presets and choose a playlist before you leave, and finish any grooming before starting out or after arriving. Make sure children are comfortable and buckled before the trip, since tending to them while driving is a serious distraction. These are all things that feel small, but each one can pull your eyes, hands or mind away. Children are the biggest of these. A child who is uncomfortable or unbuckled will need attention, and that attention is hard to give safely while driving. Deal with it in the driveway rather than on the road.

lines.text: Park safely to make a call.

narration.text: While driving, avoid phones, texting devices and navigation or other electronic systems, and if you must call, park safely first. Do not take notes, read, look up numbers or get into stressful or confrontational conversations while driving. If you eat while driving, pick easy-to-handle food and keep drinks secured in cup holders, and take a break if you feel tired or lost in thought. Notice the emotional part of that list. A heated conversation is a distraction of the mind, even if your hands and eyes seem to be in the right place.

lines.text: Finish before leaving or after arriving.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some people believe it is fine to do small tasks at red lights or in slow traffic, like finishing grooming or scrolling for a song. The handbook places those tasks before you start out or after you arrive. Grooming belongs before the trip or after it, and music choices belong before you leave. The same idea applies to phone calls. If a call cannot wait, the handbook's answer is to park safely first, not to make it at a stop light. When a question offers a during-the-drive shortcut, look for the before or after option.

Here is a quick check: you are about to leave the driveway, and your child in the back seat is fussing with the seat belt. When should you get them comfortable and buckled? The answer is before the trip starts. Tending to children while driving is a serious distraction, so the handbook asks you to make sure they are comfortable and buckled before you go. Reaching back at a red light or while moving takes your eyes, your hands and your mind away from driving. A few minutes in the driveway prevents all of that. The road is not the place to catch up on tasks.

To wrap up the habits, prepare before the trip: have a passenger handle navigation or plan your route, learn your controls, set presets and playlists, finish grooming, and make sure children are comfortable and buckled. While driving, avoid phones and electronic systems, and park safely first if you must call. Do not take notes, read, look up numbers or get into stressful conversations. If you eat, choose easy food and secure your drinks, and take a break if you feel tired or lost in thought. Park before you call. That is the safest choice.

why_how.text: Michigan's general cell phone law bars every driver from holding or using a mobile device on public roads, with an emergency exception.
The fines rise after the first offense, so repeat violations cost more.

scenario.text: Jordan is caught holding a phone to read a text, and it is Jordan's second violation.

reasoning.text: A first hand-held phone offense costs one hundred dollars, and every later one costs two hundred fifty dollars.

result.text: Jordan's fine is two hundred fifty dollars.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking teens may not use a phone even to report a crash.

correction.text: Any driver, including a teen, may text nine-one-one or call emergency services to report a medical emergency, crash, serious hazard, fire or hazardous materials incident.

prompt.text: A driver sees an apparently impaired driver weaving across lanes. May they use a phone to report it?

answer.text: Yes, reporting a reckless or apparently impaired driver is covered by the emergency exception.

rationale.text: The emergency exception covers crashes, hazards, fires and medical emergencies, plus reckless or impaired drivers and crimes in progress.

narration.text: This lesson covers Michigan's phone laws for every driver. The basic rule is simple: holding a phone while driving is illegal in Michigan, and that covers reading, texting, and making or answering a call. There are exceptions for reporting crashes, crimes or other emergencies, and there are fines when the rule is broken. Practice questions usually focus on three things: which uses are banned, which emergencies are allowed, and how much the fines are. We will go through each one, and in the next lesson we will add the special rules for teens and the uses that are allowed.

lines.text: No holding or using a device.

narration.text: Michigan's general cell phone law bars every driver from holding or using a mobile electronic device such as a phone or tablet while operating a vehicle on a public road or other public venue. Holding a phone while driving is illegal, which covers reading, texting, and making or answering a call. The law is not limited to phones. A tablet counts, and so does any similar mobile electronic device. The location matters too: public roads and other public venues. So a parking lot open to the public is not a place to start scrolling while the car is moving.

lines.text: Reading or posting to social media.

narration.text: Banned uses include sending or receiving calls, sending, receiving or reading texts, viewing, recording or transmitting video, and reading or posting to social media. That list covers almost every common phone activity. Reading a message counts, even if you do not reply. Watching a video counts, even if someone else started it. Recording a video counts too, even if it seems like you are just capturing the scenery. If you are holding or using a device for any of these while driving, you are breaking the law, unless you are in one of the emergency situations described next.

Any driver, including a teen, may use a device to text nine-one-one or call police, a health-care provider, the fire department or another emergency service to report a medical emergency, crash, serious road hazard, fire or hazardous materials incident. The emergency exception also covers reporting a reckless or apparently impaired driver, or a crime in progress. So the exception is about contacting help in a real emergency. It is not a general permission. Calling a friend to say you are late, or checking a message, is not an emergency, and the ban still applies.

lines.text: Trap: one fine for every offense.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The hand-held phone fine is not the same every time. A first hand-held phone offense costs one hundred dollars, and every later one costs two hundred fifty dollars. Options may swap the numbers or offer a single flat fine. A second trap is about teens and emergencies. Some learners think a teen may never touch a phone while driving. In fact, any driver, teens included, may contact police, fire, health-care or other emergency services, though the exception does not cover ordinary personal calls. Read who is calling and why before you answer.

Here is a quick check: you see a driver ahead weaving across lanes, and they appear to be impaired. May you use your phone to report it? Think about the emergency exception. It covers contacting emergency services for medical emergencies, crashes, serious hazards, fires and hazardous materials incidents. It also covers reporting a reckless or apparently impaired driver, or a crime in progress. So the answer is yes. Reporting that driver is exactly the kind of call the exception allows. What it does not allow is using the phone for an ordinary chat afterward.

lines.text: No holding a device to call, text, watch or post.

narration.text: To close, Michigan bars every driver from holding or using a mobile electronic device on public roads and other public venues. Banned uses include calls, texts, video and social media. Any driver, teens included, may use a device to contact emergency services about a medical emergency, crash, serious hazard, fire or hazardous materials incident, and to report a reckless or apparently impaired driver or a crime in progress. The fine is one hundred dollars for a first offense and two hundred fifty dollars for each later one. One hundred, then two fifty.

title.text: Teen phone rules and allowed uses

why_how.text: Kelsey's Law adds a stricter rule for Level one and Level two teens: no non-emergency calls, even hands-free.
Other drivers may use GPS without typing and hands-free functions that need only a single touch.

scenario.text: Kai has a Level two license and wants to answer a friend's call using the car's hands-free system.

reasoning.text: Kelsey's Law bars Level one and Level two teens from making or receiving non-emergency calls, even hands-free.

result.text: Kai may not take the call while driving.

claim.text: Many people think the emergency exception covers any call a teen needs to make.

correction.text: The emergency exception lets any driver contact police, fire, health-care or other emergency services, but it does not cover ordinary personal calls.

prompt.text: An adult driver wants to enter a new address into the navigation system while driving. Is that allowed?

answer.text: No. GPS is allowed only when you do not type information in by hand.

rationale.text: Using GPS is allowed without typing by hand, while a single tap to start or end a hands-free call is allowed.

lines.text: Kelsey's Law for Level one and two.

narration.text: This lesson adds two layers to Michigan's phone rules. First, there is a stricter rule for young drivers, called Kelsey's Law, that applies to teens holding a Level one or Level two license. Second, there are specific uses that are allowed for other drivers, such as GPS, hands-free functions, dash cams and mounted devices. Questions on this topic usually describe a driver and a device, then ask whether the use is allowed. To answer correctly, you need to know both who the driver is and exactly how the device is being used.

lines.text: Applies to Level one and Level two teens.

narration.text: Kelsey's Law bars teens holding a GDL Level one or Level two license from making or receiving non-emergency phone calls. That applies even hands-free. A teen with a Level one or Level two license may not make or take non-emergency calls through the car's system or a headset while driving. The emergency exception still applies to them, as it does to all drivers. Once a teen reaches Level three, they follow the same hands-free rules as adult drivers. So the license level is the first thing to check whenever a question involves a teen and a phone.

lines.text: GPS allowed without typing by hand.
Single press, tap or swipe allowed.

narration.text: GDL Level three teens and all other drivers may use GPS or navigation as long as they do not type information in by hand. Voice-operated or hands-free use is allowed if your hands stop after a single press, tap or swipe to start or end a function or pick a contact, or after using the vehicle's built-in interface. So following directions on a screen is fine, and starting a call with one tap is fine. Typing in a new address, or scrolling through a list with several swipes, goes beyond what is allowed. The single-touch idea is the key.

lines.text: Dash cams that record or broadcast.
Mounted devices used in exempt ways.

narration.text: A dash cam that continuously records or broadcasts video is allowed. A mounted device used in an already exempt way is also allowed. So a phone in a dashboard mount, showing navigation that you are not typing into, fits within the rules. The mount by itself does not make every use legal, though. Watching a video on a mounted phone is still viewing video, which is a banned use. The question is always what you are doing with the device, not only where it sits. Keep that in mind when an option mentions a mount as if it solves everything.

Let us connect two allowed uses that are easy to blur. Using GPS is allowed only when you do not type in information by hand, whereas a single tap to start or end a hands-free call is allowed. Both rules point to the same idea: brief, single actions are acceptable, while longer hand use is not. Typing an address takes your eyes, hands and mind for several seconds. A single tap takes much less. When a question describes a driver using a device, count the actions. One tap or swipe can be fine. Typing or scrolling is not.

lines.text: Trap: Level two teens may use hands-free.
Level one and two: no non-emergency calls.
Emergency exception is not for personal calls.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Teens with a Level one or Level two license may not make or take non-emergency calls even hands-free under Kelsey's Law, while Level three teens follow the same hands-free rules as adult drivers. Options may say Level two teens can use hands-free calls like adults. They cannot. A second trap is stretching the emergency exception. It lets any driver, teens included, contact police, fire, health-care or other emergency services, but it does not cover ordinary personal calls. A teen running late does not have an emergency, so that call must wait.

Here is a quick check: an adult driver wants to type a new address into the navigation system while the car is moving. Is that allowed? Recall the GPS rule. Drivers may use GPS or navigation as long as they do not type information in by hand. Typing an address is exactly what the rule excludes, so the answer is no. The driver could enter the address before leaving, or pull over safely and enter it then. A single tap to start or end a hands-free call would be allowed, but typing a destination is not. That is the safe choice.

lines.text: Level one and two teens: no calls.
GPS without typing; one touch allowed.

narration.text: To wrap up, Kelsey's Law bars teens with a Level one or Level two license from making or receiving non-emergency calls, even hands-free, while Level three teens follow adult rules. All other drivers may use GPS without typing by hand, and hands-free functions that stop after a single press, tap or swipe or use the built-in interface. Continuously recording dash cams are allowed, and mounted devices used in exempt ways are too. The emergency exception covers every driver for real emergencies, but never ordinary personal calls. Level one, two: no calls.

why_how.text: Buckling up is the most effective single step to protect yourself in a crash, and seat belts save more than thirteen thousand lives a year.
Air bags add protection, but only a correctly worn belt holds you in place.

scenario.text: A family of four rides together: the driver, an adult in front, and two children aged ten and fourteen in the back.

reasoning.text: The driver and every front-seat passenger must wear a seat belt, and every passenger under sixteen must be buckled in any seat.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking air bags make a seat belt unnecessary.

correction.text: Air bags add protection but never replace a belt, which belongs across the middle of the chest and low on the hips.

prompt.text: A fifteen-year-old rides in the third row of a van. Must they be buckled?

answer.text: Yes. Every passenger under sixteen must be buckled in any seat.

rationale.text: The any-seat rule covers every passenger under sixteen, wherever they sit.

narration.text: This lesson covers Michigan's seat belt rules and why they matter. We will start with enforcement, then cover who must be buckled and where they sit, why belts are so effective, how a belt should fit, and the one exception for medical reasons. Seat belt questions often test the age line for passengers in the back seat and the relationship between belts and air bags. By the end you will know exactly who has to buckle, and why an air bag is never a substitute. Let us start with what can happen when someone in the car is not buckled.

lines.text: An officer may stop you for no belt.

narration.text: Under Click It or Ticket, an officer may stop a vehicle simply because the driver or passengers are not properly buckled. You do not need to be speeding or breaking any other rule. Being unbuckled is enough reason for a stop. That makes the seat belt rule one of the most directly enforced rules in the handbook. Notice the word properly. A belt worn behind the back or under the arm is not properly buckled, so it does not satisfy the rule. Correct fit matters for safety and for the law, which is why we will look at fit shortly.

lines.text: Every passenger under sixteen, any seat.

narration.text: Michigan requires the driver and every front-seat passenger to wear a seat belt, and every passenger under sixteen to be buckled in any seat. So the front seat is simple: everyone there must buckle. In the back, the rule depends on age. Every rider under sixteen must be buckled wherever they sit, including the second or third row. Federal safety officials report seat belts save more than thirteen thousand lives a year, and buckling up is the most effective single step to protect yourself in a crash, so the safest choice is for everyone to buckle up.

lines.text: Shoulder belt mid-chest, away from neck.
Lap belt low across the hips.
Medical exemption needs a doctor's statement.

narration.text: Air bags do not replace a seat belt. Wear the shoulder belt across the middle of the chest away from the neck, and the lap belt low across the hips below the stomach. A belt across the neck or stomach can fail to hold you properly. A driver excused from wearing a seat belt for a medical reason must carry a doctor's statement. That exemption is narrow and needs proof. Without the doctor's statement, a medical reason does not excuse an unbuckled driver. So fit and documentation are the two details to remember here. Keep both in mind.

lines.text: Under sixteen buckles in any seat.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many people believe air bags make a seat belt unnecessary. Air bags add protection but never replace a belt, which belongs across the middle of the chest and low on the hips. A second trap is the back-seat age line. Every passenger under sixteen must be buckled in any seat, while for riders sixteen and older the handbook's belt rule names only the driver and front-seat passengers. Options may move that line to eighteen or to eight. The belt line is sixteen, which is different from the pickup bed and booster seat lines you will learn later.

Here is a quick check: a fifteen-year-old rides in the third row of a family van. Must they be buckled? Recall the age rule for passengers outside the front seat. Every passenger under sixteen must be buckled in any seat. Fifteen is under sixteen, and the third row is still a seat, so the answer is yes. The location in the vehicle does not matter for riders under sixteen. If the rider were in the front seat, they would need to buckle at any age, because every front-seat passenger must wear a seat belt. Age decides the back seat.

lines.text: Driver, front seat, and under sixteen anywhere.

narration.text: To finish, Click It or Ticket lets an officer stop a vehicle simply because someone is not properly buckled. The driver and every front-seat passenger must wear a belt, and every passenger under sixteen must be buckled in any seat. Seat belts save more than thirteen thousand lives a year and are the most effective single step to protect yourself. Wear the shoulder belt across the middle of the chest and the lap belt low on the hips. A medical exemption requires carrying a doctor's statement. Air bags add, never replace.

why_how.text: Children under eight, or shorter than four feet nine inches, ride in an approved car seat or booster because a belt may not fit a small child.
Placement rules protect the youngest riders: children under four in a rear seat, and rear-facing seats in front only with the air bag off.

scenario.text: Lena has a two-year-old in a rear-facing seat and a sedan with an empty back seat.

reasoning.text: Children under four must ride in a rear seat when the vehicle has one, and a rear-facing seat may go in front only when the passenger air bag is turned off.

result.text: Lena places the rear-facing seat in the back seat.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a rear-facing seat may go in the front whenever the back seat is inconvenient.

correction.text: Children under four belong in the rear seat, while a rear-facing seat may sit in front only if the passenger air bag is deactivated.

prompt.text: When does a child leave the car seat or booster, according to the handbook?

answer.text: At age eight or four feet nine inches, whichever comes first.

rationale.text: The handbook adds that parents should go by height, because a seat belt may not fit a small child.

narration.text: This lesson covers how children must ride in Michigan. We will look at who needs a car seat or booster, when a child can move to a regular seat belt, how the restraint must be installed, and where the youngest children belong in the vehicle. We will also cover a few things the handbook says never to do, such as holding a child on your lap. Child restraint questions often combine an age, a height and a seat position, so we will slow down on those combinations and make sure each rule is matched to the right child. Each rule has a reason.

lines.text: Under eight or under four feet nine inches.

narration.text: Children under eight, or shorter than four feet nine inches, must ride in an approved car seat or booster seat in every seating position. A child rides in a car seat or booster until reaching eight years old or four feet nine inches, whichever comes first, and parents are urged to go by height because a belt may not fit a small child. So the handbook gives a legal line and a safety suggestion. The suggestion exists because the adult belt is designed for a bigger body, and on a small child it can sit across the neck or stomach.

lines.text: Never unbuckle to nurse while moving.

narration.text: The child must be secured following the restraint and vehicle makers' instructions and federal safety standards. Taking a child out of a car seat to nurse while the vehicle is moving is prohibited. Both rules protect the child from the moment the car starts until it stops. Following both sets of instructions matters, because the seat and the vehicle each have their own requirements. And the nursing rule is clear: if a baby needs to nurse, stop the vehicle first. A moving car is never the place to have a child out of the restraint.

lines.text: Under four: rear seat when available.
Rear-facing in front: air bag off.

narration.text: Children under four must ride in a rear seat when the vehicle has one, unless every rear seat is already filled by children under four. A rear-facing child seat may go in the front only when the front passenger air bag is turned off. Never hold a child on your lap or share one seat belt between a child and another passenger, and have children buckle up before you start the engine. So the rear seat is the default for the youngest children, and the front is allowed only in specific situations. A lap is never a safe seat.

lines.text: Trap: front is fine when convenient.
Rear-facing in front only with air bag off.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Children under four belong in the rear seat, while a rear-facing seat may sit in front only if the passenger air bag is deactivated. An option may suggest putting a toddler up front because it is easier to reach them, or putting a rear-facing seat in front with the air bag on. Both break the rules. A second trap is the booster line. A child leaves the car seat or booster at age eight or at four feet nine inches, whichever comes first, though the handbook suggests going by height. Watch for options that use only one of the two lines.

lines.text: Never a child on your lap.

narration.text: Let us connect the placement rules to one more set of never-do items. Never hold a child on your lap, and never share one seat belt between a child and another passenger. Have children buckle up before you start the engine. These rules fill the gaps that the car seat and rear seat rules might leave. A parent might think holding a baby is safer than a seat, or that two small children can share one belt in a crowded car. Both are not allowed. Every child gets their own proper restraint, buckled before the car moves. One child, one restraint.

lines.text: When does a child leave the booster?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: according to the handbook, when does a child leave the car seat or booster seat? Recall the two lines. A child rides in a car seat or booster until reaching eight years old or four feet nine inches, whichever comes first. The handbook also urges parents to go by height, because a seat belt may not fit a small child. So the answer is age eight or four feet nine inches, whichever comes first, with height as the suggested guide. If you named only one of those lines, you have half of the rule. Both lines count.

lines.text: Car seat or booster until eight or four feet nine.

narration.text: To wrap up, children under eight or shorter than four feet nine inches ride in an approved car seat or booster in every seating position, until eight or four feet nine inches, whichever comes first, with height as the suggested guide. Secure the child by the restraint and vehicle instructions and federal standards, and never take a child out to nurse while moving. Children under four ride in a rear seat when there is one, and a rear-facing seat goes in front only with the air bag off. Never hold a child on your lap or share a belt.

title.text: Pickup beds and car seat help

why_how.text: The open pickup bed rule protects riders under eighteen at speeds above fifteen miles per hour, with specific work and emergency exceptions.
Certified help and new, standards-meeting seats make car seats work as designed.

scenario.text: A sixteen-year-old wants to ride in an open pickup bed to a friend's house at forty miles per hour.

reasoning.text: No one under eighteen may ride in an open pickup bed above fifteen miles per hour, except for farm, construction, military, parade and authorized emergency or rescue uses.

result.text: The ride is not allowed, even though the rider is over sixteen.

claim.text: Common mistake: assuming the pickup bed rule uses the same under-sixteen age line as the seat belt rule.

correction.text: Riders under eighteen may not ride in an open pickup bed above fifteen miles per hour, which is a different age line from the under-sixteen seat belt rule.

prompt.text: Why does the handbook say to avoid secondhand car seats?

answer.text: They may not meet federal standards, may not work properly, or may be missing parts or instructions.

rationale.text: A seat you cannot verify might fail in a crash, so a new seat that meets federal standards is the safer choice.

lines.text: Riding in an open pickup bed.

narration.text: This short lesson covers two final topics about passengers. The first is riding in the open bed of a pickup truck, which has its own age and speed rule with a list of exceptions. The second is getting help with car seats, including where to find a certified technician and why the handbook warns against secondhand seats. Both topics include details that practice questions like to twist, such as an age line that sounds like the seat belt rule but is not the same. We will make sure each number is attached to the right rule.

lines.text: No riders under eighteen above fifteen miles per hour.

narration.text: No one under eighteen may ride in an open pickup bed above fifteen miles per hour, except for farm, construction, military, parade and authorized emergency or rescue uses. So both age and speed matter. A rider under eighteen at highway speed in an open bed is breaking the rule, unless one of the listed uses applies. A parade moving slowly or a farm task fits the exceptions. A trip to a friend's house does not. When a question describes a pickup bed rider, check the rider's age, the speed, and whether the purpose is on the exception list.

lines.text: Certified technicians at the safe kids site.

narration.text: Help installing a car seat is available from community agencies such as local health departments, and a certified technician can be found at cert dot safekids dot org under Find a Tech. Avoid secondhand car seats, which may not meet federal standards, may not work properly, or may be missing parts or instructions. A seat you cannot verify may not protect a child the way it should. Getting help from a certified technician makes sure the seat you have is installed correctly, and choosing a seat that meets standards makes sure the seat itself can do its job.

lines.text: Trap: pickup beds use under sixteen.
Seat belts in any seat: under sixteen.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Riders under eighteen may not ride in an open pickup bed above fifteen miles per hour, which is a different age line from the under-sixteen seat belt rule. Because both rules are about young passengers, it is easy to move one number into the other rule. A sixteen-year-old must still follow the pickup bed rule, even though the any-seat belt rule no longer names them. And a fifteen-year-old must be buckled in any seat, which is a separate requirement. Keep eighteen with pickup beds and sixteen with the any-seat belt rule.

lines.text: Why does the handbook warn against it?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a neighbor offers you a free used car seat. Why does the handbook say to avoid secondhand car seats? Recall the three concerns. A secondhand seat may not meet federal standards, may not work properly, or may be missing parts or instructions. Any one of those could keep the seat from protecting a child in a crash. So the handbook's advice is to avoid it. If you do have a seat, community agencies and certified technicians can help you install it correctly, and the safe kids site lists technicians under Find a Tech.

To close, no one under eighteen may ride in an open pickup bed above fifteen miles per hour, except for farm, construction, military, parade and authorized emergency or rescue uses. That under-eighteen line is different from the under-sixteen seat belt rule. For car seats, community agencies such as local health departments can help with installation, and certified technicians are listed at the safe kids site under Find a Tech. Avoid secondhand car seats, which may not meet federal standards, may not work properly, or may be missing parts or instructions.
